structured_output.hypothesis: If the claim holds, the reconstructed 3D surface of normal biconcave human red cells has mean curvature H that varies substantially across the surface (not constant), with the biconcave dimple having H of opposite sign to the rim, so it is not a constant-mean-curvature surface, and cells in hypotonic or diluted medium become near-spherical (sphericity close to 1).
structured_output.pass_criterion: In at least 90% of normal discocyte surfaces (n≥100) the coefficient of variation of mean curvature over the membrane surface exceeds 0.5, with H changing sign between dimple and rim, and the best-fit constant-mean-curvature (Delaunay or sphere) surface has RMS radial deviation above 10% of the cell radius. In the same dataset, cells in hypotonic medium have a median sphericity (isoperimetric ratio 36πV²/A³) above 0.9.
structured_output.fail_criterion: The claim is refuted if more than 25% of normal discocytes have a mean-curvature CV below 0.2 with no sign change, or are fit by a constant-mean-curvature surface with RMS deviation below 5% of the cell radius, or if hypotonic cells keep a median sphericity below 0.8.
structured_output.interpretation: Thompson's "surface of equilibrium" under surface tension alone means a surface of constant mean curvature (Plateau/Delaunay). Modern measurement uses 3D reconstructed cell surfaces, meaning segmented confocal or holographic images or meshes, from which curvature is computed. His "diluted blood" is osmotic swelling in hypotonic medium. Modern reinterpretation: the red cell membrane resists bending and has a spectrin cytoskeleton, so Helfrich bending energy and area-difference elasticity govern its shape, not surface tension alone. The test checks only the geometric part of the claim (non-constant H), not the proposed alternative forces (osmotic inequilibrium, liquid-crystal cholesterin).
structured_output.no_dataset_reason: I could not verify a specific public repository record of 3D red blood cell surfaces, with and without hypotonic treatment, under a URL or DOI I am sure resolves. Searches turned up a 3D confocal RBC study (Simionato et al., 825 cells), but no verifiable repository landing page, and the Zenodo RBC records found were 2D image datasets, which cannot give a surface mean curvature. I am leaving the dataset null rather than risk an invented identifier.
